title: Creation and motion of antiferromagnetic skyrmions by edge manipulation
authors: Aleksey Berg, Tim Matthies, Roland Wiesendanger, Elena Y. Vedmedenko
abstract: Magnetic racetrack architectures that use topological magnetic particles to store information are one of the most promising concepts for future storage applications. Antiferromagnetic racetracks are particularly appealing as they are not susceptible to external magnetic fields. State-of-the-art racetracks use magnetic fields, spin-transfer and spin-orbit torques caused by electric currents to move the bits across the entire circuit. However, the application of currents in many antiferromagnetic racetracks is limited because many of them are insulating. Recently, however, a concept for ferromagnetic racetrack memories that are free of global driving forces has been proposed. It has been demonstrated that various topological entities can be generated and transported over long distances solely through local magnetization rotation at the sample boundaries, independent of global driving forces. Here, we demonstrate that the local rotation of magnetization at the boundary of an antiferromagnetic sample can be exploited in racetracks to efficiently generate and transmit antiferromagnetic skyrmions. Additionally, we demonstrate that local switching of staggered magnetization at the edge of an antiferromagnetic racetrack can be even more successful than the rotational procedure. A comparison of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic processing of skyrmionic bits, together with energy considerations, shows that this procedure is fairly efficient in antiferromagnets.
summary: This work demonstrates that antiferromagnetic skyrmions can be efficiently created and moved in magnetic racetracks solely by manipulating the local magnetization at the sample edges. By comparing these results to ferromagnetic counterparts, the authors show that AFM systems offer superior performance, particularly regarding operational frequency limits and energy efficiency for this boundary-driven process.
main_problem: The research aims to develop efficient, current-free methods for generating and transporting topological magnetic skyrmions within antiferromagnetic (AFM) racetrack architectures.
main_result: Local manipulation of the magnetization at the sample boundary—either through smooth rotation or switching—can efficiently generate and move AFM skyrmions, showing advantages over ferromagnetic counterparts in terms of frequency limits and robustness.
method: The study uses atomistic simulations based on the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, analyzing the dynamics using analytical approximations like the Thiele equation for skyrmion motion.
model_or_system: The system is an AFM racetrack modeled on a lattice, governed by an effective Hamiltonian derived from the underlying magnetic interactions. Dynamics are simulated by applying local boundary fields ($\mathbf{B}_{	ext{edge}}$) that drive magnetization rotation or switching.
key_observables: Skyrmion position ($d$ vs $t$), propagation velocity ($\mathbf{v}_x$), skyrmion number ($|N_T|$), and the energy cost required for creation ($\Delta H_{	ext{skyr}}$).
important_parameters:
Edge field amplitude ($\mathbf{B}_{	ext{edge}}$), rotation frequency ($
u$), racetrack width ($N_y$), and material parameters like exchange coupling ($J$) and DMI constants.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes adiabatic changes during edge field manipulation and compares results between FM and AFM systems, noting that the AFM case exhibits unique directional requirements for optimal switching.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate skyrmion positions after boundary rotation (Fig. 1), compare time-dependent displacement and velocity for FM vs. AFM under rotating fields (Fig. 2), map stable creation regions in parameter space (Fig. 3), and show frequency limitations for both types of skyrmions (Fig. 4).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical motivation (AFM racetracks avoiding global currents), then detailing the simulation methods using edge field manipulation, presenting comparative results between FM and AFM dynamics under rotation/switching, and finally quantifying the energy efficiency of the process.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the controlled manipulation of topological excitations (skyrmions) via boundary conditions and non-global driving forces shares conceptual links with controlling quantum states in engineered systems, making it relevant to understanding dissipation and state preparation in open quantum systems.
